newsitem.title: USA: Suspected former Nazi guard hurt in shootout.
newsitem.headline: Suspected former Nazi guard hurt in shootout.

text.p: A suspected former Nazi concentration camp guard being investigated by the U.S. Justice Department was shot and wounded on Tuesday after firing gunshots at police and reporters, police said.

The confrontation began when reporters descended on Michael Kolnhofer's home in this quiet Kansas City, Missouri, suburb after the Justice Department said it had begun proceedings to revoke his U.S. citizenship.

Kolnhofer, 79, talked briefly with reporters and admitted he had been a camp guard, then began yelling at them and brandished a handgun, pulling the trigger of the unloaded weapon at one point, WDAF-TV reporter Teri Schaefer said.
"He started yelling at me in a heavy German accent and I couldn't understand what he said," Schaefer told viewers later.

Witnesses said Kolnhofer loaded the weapon inside his home by the time police arrived, and fired several shots at officers and reporters from his porch before police returned fire and wounded him in the right leg.
Kolnhofer was in serious but stable condition at the University of Kansas Medical Centre, a hospital spokeswoman said.

"The guy comes out of his house wielding a gun and telling people to leave. The police showed up and the man fired several shots at the officers. Fortunately he didn't hit anybody," Kansas City Police spokesman Don Denny said.

In a news release issued earlier the Justice Department's Nazi-hunting Office of Special Investigations said it had begun proceedings to revoke Kolnhofer's citizenship, charging that he concealed his identity when he immigrated to the United States in 1952.
"He never would have received a U.S. visa had he disclosed the truth," Eli Rosenbaum, director of the Office of Special Investigations, said.

Kolnhofer has worked in construction jobs in the Kansas City area and lived at one time in Florida, according to local attorney Robert DeCoursey. He said Kolnhofer came to see him about 10 days ago about the pending Justice Department action.
DeCoursey said Kolnhofer's wife was dead and he had no children. Neighbours described him as a friendly man who offered them vegetables from the garden he tended.

The Justice Department complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Kansas City charged Kolnhofer with taking part in Nazi atrocities while serving as an SS guard at concentration camps in wartime Germany. It alleged Kolnhofer joined the German Waffen-SS in September 1942 and served as an armed guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp near Berlin until January 1944.
To enter the United States Kolnhofer claimed he served in the German army in Russia from 1942 to 1943.

Tens of thousands of Jews and other prisoners died at Sachsenhausen, the site of some of the most gruesome Nazi medical experiments on prisoners. The Justice Department said Kolnhofer later transferred to Buchenwald, a concentration camp near Weimar, Germany, where thousands were murdered by hanging, shooting, lethal injection and other means.

To date 57 people with pasts involving Nazi persecution have been stripped of U.S. citizenship. A total of 49 have been removed from the United States since the Office of Special Investigations began operations in 1979. More than 300 people are under investigation, the Justice Department said.
